content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken without skin is a lean source of protein obtained by slow cooking the meat in liquid. The skin is removed, which reduces fat and calorie content while preserving the meat’s nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is the most widely consumed poultry worldwide and features in virtually every cuisine.
Stewing retains more B‑vitamins compared with frying.
Skin‑less chicken contains roughly half the calories of the same cut with skin.
The slow cooking process converts collagen into gelatin, giving the dish a rich, silky texture.
Stewed chicken is a staple in traditional dishes such as Russian "Kurochka v smetane" and French "Coq au vin".

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated fat dramatically, making it heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It is a good source of phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Stewed meat is tender and gentle on the stomach, suitable for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals can be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding large amounts of salt to the broth can raise sodium levels; season moderately.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed skin‑less chicken can be served on its own, added to soups, stews, salads, pasta, or used as a filling for pies. It pairs well with vegetables, whole grains and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked chicken within 2 hours, then place in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to 75 °C before serving.

green-peas-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked-.title: Green peas, canned, reduced sodium, cooked with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas with reduced sodium are cooked in their own juice with added butter or margarine. The product retains a bright color, a delicate flavor and a slightly firm texture, while the lower salt content makes it suitable for sodium‑restricted diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas are an excellent source of plant protein and dietary fiber.
Canning preserves most of the B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
Reduced sodium is achieved through specialized processing and limited added salt.
Peas are used in traditional dishes worldwide, from French ragouts to Indian dal.
Cooking with butter enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin K.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients support red blood cell formation and cellular metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt makes the product suitable for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Added fat
items.content: Because the peas are cooked with butter, calorie‑conscious consumers should account for the extra fat.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain batches may contain preservatives that can cause sensitivity in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or mashed into a puree. They pair well with boiled potatoes, carrots, and meat dishes. For extra flavor, briefly sauté in a pan with a little more butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep the peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration develops.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-made-with-whole-or-r.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa made with whole or reduced‑fat (2 %) milk

content.title: About
content.content: Hot chocolate or cocoa prepared with whole or reduced‑fat (2 %) milk is a beverage made from cocoa powder, sugar and milk. It offers a rich chocolate flavor, creamy texture and a warming effect, making it a favorite during colder months.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is derived from fermented and roasted cacao beans.
The tradition of drinking hot chocolate originated in Central and South America, where cacao was used in ceremonial drinks.
Adding milk softens the bitterness of cocoa and increases the calcium and vitamin D content of the drink.
In the United States hot chocolate is often topped with whipped cream, marshmallows or a sprinkle of cinnamon.
There are many variations: spiced (cinnamon, ginger), flavored (vanilla, mint) or made with plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The milk component provides a substantial amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing compounds
items.content: Phenylethylamine and theobromine in cocoa may improve mood and boost energy.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in cocoa supports muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Warm milk helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercial mixes often contain high amounts of added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant should use lactose‑free or plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to cocoa components.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains modest levels of stimulants that may affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Combine 2–3 tablespoons cocoa powder with 1 teaspoon sugar, add a splash of hot water and whisk to a smooth paste. Pour in 250 ml of milk (whole or 2 %); heat gently while stirring until steaming. Optionally add a pinch of salt, vanilla extract or cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep milk refrigerated and use within 5–7 days after opening.

hot-dog-sandwich-turkey-on-white-bun.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, Turkey, on White Bun

content.title: About
content.content: A sandwich consisting of sliced cooked turkey placed in a soft white bun and topped with classic condiments such as mustard, ketchup and pickles. It is often offered in cafeterias and fast‑food outlets as a lighter alternative to the traditional beef hot dog.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey provides roughly half the fat of beef while delivering a comparable amount of protein.
The white bun is typically made from wheat flour, water, yeast and a touch of sugar, giving it a soft, slightly sweet texture.
The classic American hot dog appeared in the early 1920s; the turkey version was introduced later to meet demand for healthier fast‑food options.
Pickles add not only flavor but also a small amount of probiotics.
The sandwich is convenient to eat on the go, making it popular in school cafeterias and sporting events.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey is an excellent source of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, turkey contains less saturated fat, which is better for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey provides niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals are important for immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Moderate calorie count
items.content: When consumed in reasonable portions, the sandwich supplies energy without excessive calories.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ketchup, mustard and pickles can raise the sodium level, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten in the bun
items.content: The white bun contains wheat, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor harmful bacteria, so it should be heated to a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the turkey in a microwave or skillet, split the bun, spread mustard and ketchup, add pickles and optionally lettuce or a slice of cheese. Enjoy while hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Store turkey and bun separately to prevent the bun from becoming soggy. Reheat to at least 74 °C before eating.

ripe-plantain-meat-pie-puerto-rican-styl.title: Ripe Plantain Meat Pie, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Ripe plantain meat pie is a classic Puerto Rican dish, known locally as “pastelón.” It layers fried or baked ripe plantain slices with a savory meat filling—usually ground beef or pork seasoned with garlic, adobo, olive oil, and Caribbean spices. The assembled pie is baked until the top is golden and crisp, delivering a sweet‑savory flavor profile typical of the island’s cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantains are relatives of bananas but are used when fully ripe, giving a sweet, caramelized taste.
The name “pastelón” literally means “pie” in Spanish.
Traditional recipes add a tomato‑based sauce with olives and capers for a subtle tang.
It is a staple at holidays and family gatherings, symbolizing hospitality.
Healthier versions may use turkey instead of beef and replace some oil with coconut oil.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Ripe plantains provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The combination of meat and plantain supplies vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The meat filling delivers complete protein with all essential amino acids.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Plantains contain carotenoids and phenolic compounds that combat oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because the dish uses oil and meat, portion control is important for calorie‑conscious diets.

items.title: Allergy to seafood
items.content: Some variations include shrimp or other seafood; people with allergies should verify ingredients.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salt, soy sauce, and adobo can raise sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella or Campylobacter contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie hot, cut into individual portions. It can be enjoyed on its own or alongside rice, beans, and a fresh salad. Leftovers reheat well in the oven, preserving the crisp top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the pie completely, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat in a 180 °C oven before serving to restore the crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup and broth are liquid dishes obtained by simmering meat, fish, poultry, vegetables, or a combination thereof. They serve as a flavorful base for many recipes, providing aroma, nutrients, and a warming effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of making broths dates back several millennia and appears in cultures from ancient China to medieval Europe.
In 1905 Russia began mass‑producing bone broths for therapeutic diets, calling them "liquid gold".
Broths can be clear (classic) or thick (e.g., cream soups), depending on the thickening method used.
Classic French consommé is clarified by removing fat and impurities through a filtration process.
Soups are often served with garnishes such as noodles, rice, grains, or fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Bone broths contain gelatin, which converts to collagen during digestion, supporting joint and skin health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Simmering bones and vegetables releases calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for bones and nerve function.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Soups are mostly water, helping maintain the body's fluid balance.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm liquid foods are digested quickly, making them beneficial during colds or post‑surgery recovery.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Contains amino acids (glycine, proline) that contribute to the synthesis of immune proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared soups are often salted; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Contamination if stored improperly
items.content: Broth left at room temperature for more than 2 hours can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Soups based on seafood or dairy may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Excess saturated fat
items.content: Broths made from fatty cuts of meat can contain high levels of saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve soups hot, often with herbs, spices, noodles, rice, or vegetable pieces. They can be enjoyed on their own or used as a base for more complex dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the broth to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry Milk, Fat Free (skim) is a beverage made from cow's milk with natural strawberry flavor added. The skim version contains less than 0.5 % fat, making it a low‑calorie choice for those watching their fat intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The strawberry flavor is derived from concentrated fresh‑strawberry extract or natural flavorings.
Fat‑free milk retains most B‑vitamins and calcium but has lower levels of fat‑soluble vitamins A and D.
In the US and Europe, strawberry milk is often marketed as a children's drink, but it is suitable for adults seeking variety.
Strawberries are rich in vitamin C and antioxidants, though some are lost during processing.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Even without fat, the milk provides a high amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: A serving delivers about 8 g of protein with minimal fat, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Vitamin C from strawberries
items.content: The strawberry flavor adds a modest amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Milk is roughly 90 % water, helping to maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Limited added sugar
items.content: Most commercial versions keep added sugar low, making it suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Like any cow's milk, it contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to this product.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some brands add sugar for taste; those monitoring blood sugar should check the label.

items.title: Reduced fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Skim processing lowers the natural levels of vitamins A and D found in whole milk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberry milk can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, added to smoothies, cereals, oatmeal, or used as a base for desserts. Fresh berries can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.
